en: When they saw Kanykei,
Tears poured from their eyes.
When she saw these orphans,
Your dear mother Kanykei,
Her heart torn apart,
Tears pouring from her eyes,
Her ribs coming apart,
Tears pouring from her eyes,
Unable to sniff back her running nose,
Unable to wipe away her tears,
Cried out at the sight of the orphans.
From her dear quail-like eyes,
Tears fell in separate streams.
“A spring wailing from the valley,” she said,
“A long-awaited orphan,” she said,
“Hooves left by swift steeds,
Lights left by hawks,
For twelve years I kept myself alive,
Bearing worry and sorrow for you.
Of you two orphans together,
I kept asking, ‘When shall I care for them?’”
So said Kanykei.
Of sixty thousand horses in the foothills,
She had them driven in by nineties;
Six hundred white-gray mares
She had offered in sacrifice.
Devising what no one else could imagine,
For Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
For those two she held a feast.
Argyn and Kyrgyz together
Settled there—did you see?
Kumys by day, girls by night—
So it became—did you see?
As though bloodthirsty Manas were alive,
Along this Talas
Every kind of abundance
Filled the land—did you see?!
Then the orphan, Manas's son,
On a great carpet woven of gold,
They placed him on that mighty carpet,
Set a golden crown upon him,
Seated him upon a golden throne,
Saying, “Amen!” over Talas,
They raised him as their khan.
The orphan returned, grown to maturity,
Joined his people in this way;
Manas's son, the leopard,
Now became a sultan!
Of forty young mares that had never foaled,
Your dear mother Kanykei
Had the finest slaughtered;
“May his heart be rich with fat,” she said,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro—
Feeding both to their fill,
Never letting them feel they were orphans,
Cutting belly fat and giving them neck fat,
Pouring spirits and giving them honey,
Your lion mother Kanykei
Cared for the boys like this.
Baring her right breast,
Your formidable mother Kanykei
Nursed Kulchoro;
Baring her left breast,
Your protecting mother Kanykei
Nursed Kanchoro.
From the right breast Kulchoro suckled
Pure first milk came out;
From the side Kanchoro suckled
Dark, dusky blood came out.
When she saw this sign,
The life went out of Kanykei:
“This Kulchoro here
Is your steed who will never turn away,
Until Judgment Day
Your kinsman who will go beside you.
From my side that Kanchoro suckled
Dark, dusky blood came out.
All twelve parts of my body ached;
The life went out of wretched me.
My silk wound in a skein—
When I unwind the skein, it will not separate.
This accursed Kanchoro,
If he lives and grows up,
Does not look like a boy who will walk straight.
Green-mottled silk—
When I tear it lengthwise, it will not separate.
If somehow he grows up,
He does not look like one who will belong among us!”
As he suckled at her breast,
Your mother suffered terribly;
Her eighty veins throbbed with pain,
His enmity became apparent.
“My precious orphan, heed my words:
Measuring poison in a ladle,
Giving water with a spoon,
This boy standing here—
Perhaps we should put him to death!
Low-lying mist on a black mountain
Will not part when the breeze blows.
Unless you somehow take precautions,
Unless you put him to death,
He does not look like a boy who will behave.”
Then Semetey said this:
“Who should hear these words of yours?
Let a dark night hear them.
Let a dug, dark grave hear them;
Who else should hear them!
From my second father Chubak,
From the heroic khan himself,
Kanchoro was left as a gift.
If I did that, how could I show my face?!
‘Manas's son Semetey
Is a beast,’ would they not say?
‘Between beast and human,
Rather than lay a hand on the boy,
May I perish as though never born;
Rather than live in fear of the boys,
Let me die instead of living!
Kulchoro and Kanchoro—
Both are my kinsmen.
Telling me to kill a young boy—
What were you doing just now?”
Thus the orphan would not consent.
His fortunes were complete,
He became a lion like his father.
He wore a golden crown,
He mounted a golden throne,
Readied fourteen swift horses,
Prepared a coat no bullet could pierce,
Summered in the middle of Keng-Kol,
Growing stronger as he neared exhaustion,
He became an upright, outstanding hero;
His deeds turned out right,
He became a khan like Manas,
A house built for Talas,
Splitting a black hair exactly in two,
He became a man of noble qualities.
Riding horses far, scouting the land,
Loosing dogs and flying hunting birds,
When bored, they hunted roe deer;
When not bored, in Talas
They played at their ease.
Argyn and Kyrgyz together
Settled along Keng-Kol,
As though the hero Manas, the fierce wolf,
Were still alive.
Along Zhylgyndy, Keng-Kol, broad Talas
They settled and spent the summer.
Even those called the very poorest
Tethered a thousand mares apiece;
Their daughters-in-law tethered young camels,
Their old women chewed tail fat,
They settled in bustling prosperity,
As though Manas were still alive.
In Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
While the Kyrgyz lived at ease,
He who dwelt in broad Tashkent,
Called a stately hero,
Who would yield to no one,
Who bore a gray-mottled crescent banner,
Who rode a gray, swift stallion,
Who sharpened his tongue,
Who spoke eloquently before the khan,
Who spread his white beard,
Who understood the patterns of speech,
A fluent orator, skilled in reasoning—
Khan Baimyrza had died.
The world from which no one returns—
That elder had seen it.
His fine mustache lay flat,
He set out toward Judgment Day;
His large eyes rolled,
He set out toward the other world.
He was ninety-five years old,
An elder who had seen life fully.
Consulting the elders,
His uncle Bakai, bringer of good fortune,
A sultan like Sary Khan,
Kanykei among the aged,
Chyiyrdy among the old,
Zhamgyrchy from the Eshtek—
He gathered the wise khans.
On the marsh of Uiyurmo
They assembled in a crowd;
On the marsh of Chogulma
They stood gathered together.
They laid the matter before them,
Reasoned with one another,
Matched their wits and found agreement,
Dear Bakai began to speak:
“When one travels a six-month journey,
Riding far without sparing the horse,
A noble, white-blazed steed is best.
Though he splits your lungs and takes your gall,
A kinsman's presence is a comfort.
He is a cliff no goose can circle;
Your kinsman, your support,
When you look, is a mighty mountain.
My support, my orphan, hear my words:
Let us provide six swift horses,
Give a letter the size of a palm,
To our kinsmen Abyke and Kobosh
Let us send word without stint;
Let us take this into consideration.
Whether a kinsman is truly a kinsman,
Let us find out in this way,
Then let us bury Baimyrza.
Not tiring if ridden six months,
Let us take him for our steed;
Abyke and Kobosh—
Let us take them for our kin.
Along much of broad Talas,
If they come in a mass and settle,
Along the banks of broad Keng-Kol,
If we spread out and settle,
Would any with thumbs dare approach?
Would any with claws touch me?
Would an enemy come along the road?”
Bakai said this as he stood.
Kanykei stood and said this:
“The crooked one among the forty companions—
Has that old wretch Kyrgylchal died?
Unless that old wretch dies,
Unless he sees Judgment Day,
That villain, the fool Kyrgylchal, will not disappear.
While that fool remains,
The six men's conduct will not improve.
Kyrgylchal and the forty companions—
There will be malice in their eyes.
If they have the power, those dogs
Will strike you down.
There will be difference in their eyes,
Estrangement in their words;
Devising schemes of their own,
If they have the power, these dogs
Will seek to divide you off.
Unless that swine Kyrgylchal dies,
Unless he sees Judgment Day,
Broad Talas will be no homeland for us;
Your six uncles will be no kin to us.”
Though his mother said these words,
The wretched orphan would not consent.
Generation after generation,
Fierce wolves who would not obey—
Descendants of the disobedient—
He would not consent when his mother spoke.
Your hero, brave Semetey,
Would not heed her words.
Uncle Khan Sary Khan—
To his six uncles Semetey
Decided to send him galloping as a messenger.
The twisted brass spear
He took from the corner and swung about;
He dressed him in a coat no bullet could pierce,
Mounted him on a horse no bullet could catch,
Your uncle with eyes like bowls,
